Statistical significance determines if research results are likely real or just due to chance. It is measured using p-values, typically with a threshold (alpha) of 0.05. If the p-value is below 0.05, the result is likely not random, allowing researchers to reject the null hypothesis.
the hypothesis that there is no significant difference between specified populations, any observed difference being due to sampling or experimental error.

A p-value measures the probability that observed study results occurred by random chance, assuming the null hypothesis (no real effect) is true. It ranges from 0 to 1, with a smaller p-value providing stronger evidence against the null hypothesis, typically rejecting it if. While common for determining statistical significance, p-values do not measure the size or practical importance of an effect.
